body: Poland has long white plates with the standard European blue strip on the left. Newer electric vehicles have green plates.

Polish bollards have a red strip that wraps all the way around. They have a red reflector on the front and a white reflector on the back. This design can also be found in Zakarpattia Oblast in Ukraine.

Poland uses thin concrete holey poles where the holes often don't go to the bottom. Sometimes poles are joined together or in an A-frame shape. These are distinct from the wider Hungarian and Romanian poles where holes go to the ground.
Poland has all-white road lines, and double middle lines are very common. While not unique, this is a good clue for Poland.
Poland uses square (B-type) guardrails with circular red reflectors. This type of guardrail is not very common in Europe.
Polish warning signs are triangular with a yellow background and a distinct, thin red border. This combination is unique in Europe.
Prohibitory signs in Poland are round with a white background and a thicker red border.
Poland's unique pedestrian sign has a single horizontal line instead of zebra stripes. This differs from Austria and Belgium which use two lines.
Polish direction signs have a green background and a distinct font. Signs on expressways have a blue background.
Poland has two town entry signs: a green one with the town name, and a white and black one showing a stylized urban area. Both use a distinct font.
Polish chevrons are white with red arrows.
The Polish language uses unique letters like Ł, Ą, Ę, Ń, and Ż. It is consonant-heavy, and notably uses 'W' instead of 'V'.
Poland is a generally flat country with rolling hills, a lot of agriculture, and green landscapes. Mountains can be found near the southern border.
Many roads in Poland are lined by rows of trees.
Neatly tiled sidewalks are very common in Poland, often with grey or light red tiles. Sometimes even roads are tiled.
Polish architecture includes light or pastel stucco buildings with tidy, often plastic-like roofing. Detached single-family homes and renovated communist-era apartment blocks are common.
As a very Catholic country, Christian shrines are often found on roadsides. You may also see blue-white and yellow-white Polish Catholic flags.
The first digit of 3-digit regional road numbers is often region-specific, providing a good geographical clue. This pattern does not apply to 2-digit roads.
The first two digits of 9-digit Polish landline numbers are the area code. The first digit of the area code can significantly narrow down the region.
Polish place names ending in -owo are common in the north, while those ending in -ów are common in the south. Other regional endings include -ino/-yno (northwest) and -ew (centre).
While rare, bilingual signs can be found in Poland. Look for Kashubian in the north, German in the southwest (Opole), and Lithuanian, Belarusian, or Lemko near their respective borders.
While most of Poland is flat, the southern border is very hilly and even has mountains.
Traditional wooden houses are commonly found in the east of Poland, especially in Podlaskie Voivodeship.
The Tatra Mountains, Poland's highest, are located on the Slovakian border near Zakopane.
The historic downtown of Gdańsk features unique buildings inspired by Dutch Golden Age architecture, resembling Amsterdam.
The main road on the Hel peninsula is a recognizable coastal forest road with a parallel railway track.
Białystok uses turquoise street signs, with the district marked on the bottom.
Szczecin uses colourful green and blue signs, with the city district marked on the bottom.
Street signs in Poznań are mainly black, with the district marked on a blue section at the bottom.
